newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tens of thousands of Rwandan refugees turn back.
newsitem.headline: Tens of thousands of Rwandan refugees turn back.

text.p: Tanzanian troops and police turned around tens of thousands of Rwandan refugees on Friday and herded them back towards Rwanda.
Troops blocked all entrances to the camps which the refugees fled this week to avoid what they believed would be forced repatriation.
Soldiers waved sticks around but did not hit the refugees as they marshalled them back to the nearby Rwanda border.
Refugees who wanted to sit down were told to keep moving.
The head of the column was about five km (three miles) short of the frontier. One group of refugees told Reuters they wanted to stay in the camps but were told to keep going towards Rwanda.
Tens of thousands of refugees turned around and headed back towards their camps near the border earlier on Friday after Tanzanian troops and police set up roadblocks and urged them to go back.
"I'm very pleased to see a returning trend," said Anne Willem Bijleveld of the U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR) in Ngara.

"Government authorities are on the spot. It's not clear if they are returning to the camps or being directed to the border (with Rwanda)," said Bijleveld, adding field officers were out trying to gauge the size of the refugee turnaround on Friday.
A mass of refugees estimated by Reuters at more than 100,000 had turned round after earlier heading on a marathon trek to asylum in Kenya or as far south as Malawi.

"A huge mass has just turned round, tens of thousands. They are heading north towards the border and Benaco camp. It is an absolutely incredible sight right to the horizon as far as you can see," said a spokeswoman for the World Food Programme (WFP).
"The people we had been watching for the past 24 hours going southeast are now going north along the same road," she said.
"The big question is whether they will turn back into their camps or go across the border, home to Rwanda," she added.
"Go back to the camps and you will get fed. We don't want you here. We want you to go back," Tanzanian army Colonel Urbano Nguvumali told refugees on the road between Lumasi and Benaco camps.
Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, appealed to Tanzanian authorities on Thursday to redirect the refugees back towards their camps but without using force.
Aid workers said it appeared the refugees, many of them elderly, turned back peacefully as the grip of Hutu intimidators over them had been broken once they left the camps.
The refugees were loaded down with piles of belongings. A child sat on the handlebars of a bicycle clutching a duck.
U.N. aid agency officials, who had been in despair earlier on Friday at the exodus, were ecstatic as they watched the flow.
A WFP official estimated up to 50,000 refugees turned round after troops and police set up a roadblock near Lumasi camp.
"There was some chaos while the refugees decided what to do but there were no signs of shots being fired or resistance," she said. "The refugees just turned around and headed north."
"Clearly the majority had already passed and it was a last-ditch attempt but they stopped the last 40,000 to 50,000, who headed back towards the Benaco (region) camps," she added.
UNHCR earlier on Friday blamed Hutu intimidators for the exodus in defiance of UNHCR and Tanzanian instructions to all 540,000 Rwandan refugees to return home by December 31.

"This is all pure manipulation and this is what is the tragedy, a pure humanitarian tragedy," said Bijleveld, adding all seven camps in Benaco region of Ngara had already been emptied or were in the process of emptying on Friday morning.

They had more than 494,000 residents between them, including at least 59,000 Burundians, before the exodus started on Sunday. The biggest two were Benaco with 162,000 refugees and Lumasi with 113,000.

Members of the Rwandan Hutu militia, the Interahamwe, do not want to go home for fear of prosecution or reprisals for the genocide of up to a million Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994. They want the refugees to stay with them on the principle of safety in numbers.
Refugees had said they left because they believed they would be expelled by Tanzanian authorities back to Rwanda despite some Tanzanian officials saying the repatriation would be voluntary.
Ngara is about 600 km (370 miles) west of the Kenyan border and about 850 km (530 miles) northwest of the Malawi border.

Up to half a million Hutu Rwandan refugees may still be adrift in equatorial forests of eastern Zaire, where a revolt by Tutsi Zaireans drove more than 500,000 other refugees back into Rwanda last month.
